rows.reviewerNote: Read as it will be: 'Anya buys a ruler for £1.70 and a pen for £2.60. What is the total cost?' Options £4.30*, £13.30, £3.30, £5.00. It can be answered from the stem. The key £4.30 is the only correct value under any reading, and all four option values differ. Each distractor is wrong and comes from a named mistake. Pattern check: sorted, the values are 3.30, 4.30, 5.00, 13.30 (gaps 1, 0.70, 8.30). There is no evenly spaced run with the key in the middle, so the round-1 run is broken. The pair of options £1 apart (3.30 and 4.30) has the key as the larger, which is not a rule repeated across the row. £13.30 is a long way off and an estimating child can reject it, which makes it a weak distractor but not a fault. The vocabulary (ruler, pen, total cost, pounds and pence) suits a 9 to 11 year old in Britain. Notation is house style: £ with two decimal places. Precheck --from-live: 1 row touched, 1 passes every gate, 0 fail.

changes.before: Add the two prices, pounds and pence together. Seventy pence plus sixty pence makes £1.30. That carries to give £4.30 in total. A trap drops the pence zero, or the carried pound.
changes.after: Add the two prices, pounds and pence together. Seventy pence plus sixty pence makes £1.30. That carries to give £4.30 in total. A trap loses the carried pound, or counts it as ten pounds.
Add the two prices, pounds and pence together. Seventy pence plus sixty pence makes £1.30. That carries to give £4.30 in total. A trap drops the pence zero, or the carried pound.
The child adds 70p and 60p to make 130p, writes 30p, and counts the carried 1 as a full £10 instead of £1: 10 + 1 + 2 = 13. That gives £13.30 instead of £4.30.
The child adds 70p and 60p to make 130p but keeps only the 30p and drops the carried £1, adding whole pounds 1 + 2 = 3. That gives £3.30 instead of £4.30.
The child rounds £1.70 up to £2 and £2.60 up to £3 and gives the rounded total, £5.00. The real prices are 30p and 40p less, so the total is £4.30.
